questions.title: Does the entropy model's computation count towards the total inference FLOPs in BLT?
questions.question_body: I'm trying to understand the efficiency gains of the Byte Latent Transformer. The paper claims that BLT is more efficient during inference because it uses dynamically sized patches, meaning the large global latent transformer is invoked less often. However, to determine these patches, the model uses a 'small byte-level auto-regressive language model' to compute entropies $H(x_i)$. If this entropy model has to process every single byte to decide where the boundaries are, doesn't that add a constant overhead to the inference cost? I'm confused about whether the '50% fewer flops at inference' mentioned in the abstract already accounts for the cost of running this entropy model.

questions.title: Why is Byte-Pair Encoding (BPE) not considered an incremental patching scheme?
questions.question_body: In Section 2.4, the authors define an incremental patching scheme as one where $f_p(\pmb{x}_{<i}) = f_p(\pmb{x})_{<i}$. They state that BPE does not satisfy this property because 'the same prefix can be tokenized differently depending on the continuation sequence.' I'm struggling to visualize this. Could you provide a concrete example of a string where the tokenization of a prefix changes based on the characters that follow it, and why this prevents BPE from being used in the same way as BLT's patching during generation?

questions.title: How does the pooling function $f_{\text{bytes}}(p_j)$ work in the Local Encoder's cross-attention?
questions.question_body: I'm looking at the architecture of the Local Encoder in Section 3.2.2. The paper says the query vector $Q_j$ for a patch is initialized by pooling the byte representations corresponding to that patch: $P_{0,j} = \mathcal{E}_{C}(f_{\text{bytes}}(p_j))$. It doesn't explicitly define the pooling function $f_{\text{bytes}}$. Is this a simple average of the byte embeddings in that patch, a max-pooling operation, or something else? I'm confused about how a variable-length sequence of bytes is compressed into a single initial vector for the cross-attention mechanism.

questions.title: What is the intuition behind combining raw byte embeddings with hash $n$-gram embeddings?
questions.question_body: The Local Encoder uses a specific embedding strategy: $e_i = x_i + \sum_{n=3, \ldots, 8} E_n^{hash}(\text{Hash}(g_{i,n}))$. I understand that $x_i$ is the embedding for the single byte, but I don't quite get why we need to add embeddings for $n$-grams from size 3 up to 8. Since the local encoder is already a transformer that can attend to preceding bytes, why isn't the self-attention mechanism enough to capture this local context? What specific information does the hash-embedding provide that the transformer layers would otherwise miss?

questions.title: How does the trade-off between patch size and global model size work for a fixed inference budget?
questions.question_body: The paper mentions that BLT allows for a new dimension of scaling where one can simultaneously increase the model size and the patch size while maintaining the same inference flop budget. My understanding is that if the average patch size increases, the global latent transformer is run fewer times per document. Does this mean that the 'saved' flops from running the global model fewer times can be mathematically reallocated to increase the number of layers $l_{\mathcal{G}}$ or the hidden dimension $h_{\mathcal{G}}$ of that same global model? I'm trying to understand the formula for this trade-off—specifically, how much can I grow the model if I double the average patch size?
